decks.domain: Sharing the road: emergency vehicles, police stops, work zones, railroad crossings, streetcars and light rail

cards.front: Which approaching vehicles must you yield to, and from which directions?
cards.back: You must yield to emergency vehicles such as fire trucks, police vehicles and ambulances approaching from any direction with a light or siren on.

cards.front: What do you do when you see or hear an emergency vehicle warning?
cards.back: When you see or hear an emergency vehicle warning, move right away as close to the right side of the road as is safe and stop, but never stop inside an intersection.

cards.front: How long do you stay stopped for an emergency vehicle?
cards.back: Do not drive or stop in any way that gets in an emergency vehicle's path, and stay stopped until it has passed or an officer tells you to move.

cards.front: After an emergency vehicle passes, how far behind it must you stay?
cards.back: Once an emergency vehicle has gone by, you must keep at least five hundred feet behind it.

cards.front: How does a police vehicle signal that it wants you to stop?
cards.back: A police vehicle trying to stop you will turn on flashing lights or a siren.

cards.front: When police stop you, where and how do you pull over?
cards.back: When police stop you, pull as far to the right as is safe, stop and turn off the engine, and do not stop in an intersection or pull onto a highway's center median.

cards.front: During a police stop, what should you and your passengers do with hands and movement?
cards.back: During a police stop, keep your own movements and your passengers' movements to a minimum, keep your hands on the steering wheel, and have passengers keep their hands in plain view.

cards.front: During a police stop, when do you show documents and may you get out?
cards.back: During a police stop, show your driving privilege or registration only when the officer asks, and stay inside the vehicle unless asked to get out.

cards.front: If police stop you after dark, what light should you turn on and when?
cards.back: If a police stop happens after dark, turn on the interior light once you have stopped and before the officer reaches you.

cards.front: Why should you not argue with the officer at a traffic stop?
cards.back: Do not argue with the officer at a stop, because traffic violations and traffic crimes charged against you are decided in court.

cards.front: How does pulling over for an emergency vehicle differ from a police stop?
cards.back: For an emergency vehicle you pull right and stay stopped until it passes or an officer waves you on, while for a police stop you also turn off the engine and keep your hands on the wheel.

cards.front: Where may you not stop when pulling over for police, beyond an intersection?
cards.back: Pulling over for an emergency vehicle, avoid stopping in an intersection; pulling over for police, also avoid stopping in an intersection or on a highway center median.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: emergency vehicles, police stops, work zones, railroad crossings, streetcars and light rail

cards.front: How are work zones marked, and who may be close to traffic?
cards.back: Work zones are marked by orange traffic control devices, and workers and construction equipment may be working close to traffic.

cards.front: What happens to traffic fines in a work zone, and whom do you yield to?
cards.back: Traffic fines are doubled in every work zone, and drivers are expected to yield to workers.

cards.front: What guides you through a work zone, and what do orange signs and cones do?
cards.back: Signs, cones, flaggers and lane markings guide you through a work zone; orange signs warn of what is ahead and orange cones steer you away from the construction.

cards.front: When does a temporary work zone speed apply?
cards.back: A temporary speed posted in a work zone applies at all times, even when no workers can be seen.

cards.front: What ends the lower work zone speed limit?
cards.back: The lower work zone limit holds until a sign ends it, either an End Work Zone Speed Limit sign or a different posted speed limit.

cards.front: On two-lane roads, what may stop you in a work zone and how do flaggers direct you?
cards.back: On two-lane roads, expect to be stopped in work zones by flaggers or automated devices, and flaggers use signs and hand signals to tell you which way to go, to slow or to stop.

cards.front: What is an automated flagger device and what does it have?
cards.back: An automated flagger device does the same job as a human flagger and has red and yellow lights plus a stop arm.

cards.front: At an automated flagger device, when do you stop and when do you go?
cards.back: At an automated flagger device, stop while the red light is on and the arm is lowered, and go when the yellow light flashes and the arm is raised.
cards.memory_hook: Red down stop, yellow up go

cards.front: What should you expect in a freeway work zone?
cards.back: In a freeway work zone you usually keep driving through it, but lanes may be fewer, narrower or newly placed, and you should expect to merge.

cards.front: Why slow down in a freeway work zone?
cards.back: Freeway work zones can put you very close to cones, workers and equipment, so slow down and pay attention.

cards.front: Should you follow construction vehicles in a work zone?
cards.back: Do not follow construction vehicles while in a work zone, and expect them to enter the road and slow traffic.

cards.front: If no workers are in sight, does the work zone speed still apply?
cards.back: A work zone with no workers in sight still carries its temporary speed limit, so an empty work zone is no reason to speed back up before the end sign.

cards.front: Does an automated flagger ever show a green light to go?
cards.back: At an automated flagger, red light with the arm down means stop, and flashing yellow with the arm up means go; it is not a green light signal.

cards.front: Where do you meet flaggers, and how do freeway work zones differ?
cards.back: Flaggers and automated flagger devices are what you meet on two-lane road work zones, while on freeways you usually keep moving through narrowed or shifted lanes.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: emergency vehicles, police stops, work zones, railroad crossings, streetcars and light rail

cards.front: What three things do you do when you see railroad crossing signs or signals?
cards.back: When you see railroad crossing signs or signals, look, listen and slow down, because you may need to stop.

cards.front: What does a railroad advance sign tell you?
cards.back: A railroad advance sign warns that a railroad crossing is ahead.

cards.front: What does a crossbuck assembly include, and how do you know the number of tracks?
cards.back: A railroad crossbuck assembly includes a yield or stop sign that you must obey, and where there are several tracks a sign under the crossbuck shows how many.

cards.front: What does a crossing signal system have?
cards.back: A crossing signal system has flashing red lights and may have a gate with flashing red lights that activate when a train is near.

cards.front: What pavement marking warns of a railroad crossing?
cards.back: Pavement markings at railroad crossings show a large X with the letters RR.

cards.front: When may you cross railroad tracks?
cards.back: Cross the tracks only when you are sure your vehicle can clear the crossing completely.

cards.front: What two things must you never do at a railroad crossing?
cards.back: Never stop on the tracks and never try to beat a train to a crossing.

cards.front: Why is a train more dangerous than it looks?
cards.back: A train you see is closer than it appears, and trains cannot stop quickly.

cards.front: Which vehicles must stop at every railroad crossing?
cards.back: School buses, hazmat vehicles and some school activity vehicles must stop at every railroad crossing, so be ready to stop when following one.

cards.front: Why look again after one train passes?
cards.back: One train can hide a second train from your view at a crossing.

cards.front: How does a railroad advance sign differ from a crossbuck?
cards.back: A railroad advance sign only warns that a crossing is ahead, while the crossbuck assembly at the crossing carries a yield or stop sign that you must obey.

decks.module: Stopping at crossings and getting stuck
decks.domain: Sharing the road: emergency vehicles, police stops, work zones, railroad crossings, streetcars and light rail

cards.front: Where do you stop at a railroad crossing, with and without a stop line?
cards.back: When you must stop at a railroad crossing, stop at the stop line, or if there is none, at least fifteen feet from the nearest rail.

cards.front: Which active warnings require you to stop before the tracks?
cards.back: Stop before the tracks when the flashing red lights are on, or when a train is clearly visible or so near that crossing would be hazardous.

cards.front: Must you stop at a crossing with a posted stop sign when no train is coming?
cards.back: Stop before the tracks when a stop sign is posted, even with no train in sight, and when a flagger signals you to stop.

cards.front: May you drive around or under a crossing gate?
cards.back: Driving around or under a crossing gate while it is down, rising or lowering is illegal and extremely dangerous.

cards.front: After stopping at a crossing, when may you start across?
cards.back: After stopping at a crossing, start across only when you are sure it is safe, and at multiple tracks look both ways for a second train on another track.
cards.memory_hook: Sure it is safe, look twice

cards.front: If a vehicle is stuck on the tracks, what are your first two steps?
cards.back: If a vehicle, person or object is stuck on the tracks, first get out of the vehicle, then move away from the tracks even if no train is in sight.

cards.front: How can you warn the railroad about a blockage on the tracks?
cards.back: If it is safe, find the Emergency Notification System (ENS) sign on a post near the tracks and use it to tell the railroad about the blockage so it can warn trains.

cards.front: If a train is coming while you are stuck, which way do you move away?
cards.back: If a train is coming while you are stuck, move away at a forty-five degree angle from the tracks toward the direction the train is coming from, so flying debris does not hit you.

cards.front: Which crossing condition means you stop even with no train in sight?
cards.back: A posted stop sign at a crossing means you stop even with no train in sight, while flashing red lights, a visible close train or a flagger signal are the other triggers to stop.

cards.front: When stuck on tracks, which comes first: escaping or notifying the railroad?
cards.back: If you are stuck on the tracks, getting out and away comes before notifying the railroad at the ENS sign, and notifying is done only if it is safe.

decks.domain: Sharing the road: emergency vehicles, police stops, work zones, railroad crossings, streetcars and light rail

cards.front: What are streetcars and light rail trains, and how do they use the street?
cards.back: Streetcars and light rail trains are electric transit vehicles on tracks set in the street; they sometimes share lanes with cars and stop often for passengers, much like buses.

cards.front: Who goes first, you or a streetcar, and may you pass one?
cards.back: Always let streetcars and light rail trains go first, and do not try to pass one unless it is safe.

cards.front: What do you do when a streetcar stops to let people on or off?
cards.back: When a streetcar or train stops to let people on or off, stay behind it until it moves again or the people are safely clear.

cards.front: Is a streetcar stopped for passengers a reason to pass it?
cards.back: A stopped streetcar loading passengers is a reason to stay behind it, not to pass, until it moves again or the riders are safely away.

cards.front: Approaching tracks at an intersection, where do you wait?
cards.back: Approaching tracks at an intersection, stay behind any stop line before you cross the tracks.

cards.front: Where may you park near streetcar tracks?
cards.back: Tracks are never a parking spot: leave your car behind the solid white line that marks off the track area, or where there is no line, close to the curb and as far from the rails as possible.

cards.front: What should you check before opening a door near tracks?
cards.back: Check for approaching streetcars or trains before opening a door, and make sure your parked vehicle is fully clear of the tracks.

cards.front: May you turn across a streetcar in the next lane that is moving your way or stopped?
cards.back: Never turn across the path of a streetcar or train moving your way in the next lane, even while it is stopped.

cards.front: How do you turn or cross tracks when a streetcar may approach?
cards.back: Do not turn in front of an approaching streetcar or light rail train unless it is safe, and slow down and look both ways before crossing tracks at an intersection.

cards.front: Why watch for riders near streetcar stops?
cards.back: Watch for riders near streetcar and train stops, since passengers may dash across lanes to catch one, and follow pedestrian signals so people can cross safely.

cards.front: Why check for streetcars before a lane change and avoid sudden moves?
cards.back: Check for streetcars and trains before changing lanes, since one may be close behind you, and avoid sudden braking or surprise moves around them because they cannot stop quickly.

cards.front: If your vehicle touches a streetcar, what do you do?
cards.back: If your vehicle touches a streetcar or train, wait for the operator or the police to tell you what to do.

recap_hooks.text: For a siren, pull right and stop outside intersections, then stay five hundred feet behind once it passes.
At a police stop, pull right, turn off the engine, keep hands on the wheel and stay inside.
Work zone fines are doubled and the temporary speed applies at all times, workers or not.
At an automated flagger, red with the arm down means stop and flashing yellow with the arm up means go.
The advance sign warns, the crossbuck carries a yield or stop sign, and you never stop on or race a train.

recaps.module: Stopping at crossings and getting stuck

recap_hooks.text: Stop at the stop line or at least fifteen feet from the rail, and never go around a gate.
Stuck on the tracks, get out and get away first, then use the ENS sign if it is safe.
Streetcars go first, so stay behind one that is loading and never park on the tracks.
Never turn across a streetcar in the next lane, even when it is stopped.
